title: Accessible Design Is Good Business
subtitle: Designing for people who find the web harder makes your website better for every customer, and easier for search and AI to read.
excerpt: Contrast, readable text, keyboard use, captions, dark mode, calmer motion and clear forms. Why accessible design helps every customer, plus a plain-language checklist to bring to your designer.
seoTitle: Accessible Design Is Good Business — True Love Creative
seoDescription: Why accessible, inclusive design helps every customer and your visibility in search and AI, with a plain checklist of questions to ask your web designer.
html:
When people hear “accessibility”, they often picture a compliance checklist, something for big corporations and government websites. I understand why. But after years of building sites for all kinds of businesses, I see it differently. Accessible design is simply design that works for more people, in more situations. And that turns out to be very good for business.

Think about who actually visits your website. Someone reading on their phone in bright sunlight. Someone whose eyesight isn’t what it was. Someone with a broken wrist using only the keyboard. Someone watching your video on a train with the sound off. Someone who gets dizzy when everything on the screen slides around. None of them would describe themselves as “a user with accessibility needs”. They’re just your customers, and right now some of them might be struggling.

What accessible design actually means

There is an international standard for this: the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, usually called WCAG, published by the W3C, the body that looks after web standards. It’s technical, but the ideas behind it are common sense. People should be able to see your content, understand it, move around it whichever way they use a device, and rely on it working with the tools they use, like screen readers (software that reads the page aloud).

You don’t need to read the standard. You need to know enough to ask your designer the right questions. So here are the areas that matter most, in plain language.

The areas that make the biggest difference

Contrast you can actually read

Light grey text on a white background looks elegant in a presentation and becomes unreadable on a phone outdoors. Good contrast between text and background is the cheapest accessibility win there is, and it helps literally everyone. WCAG sets minimum contrast levels, and a good designer checks them as a habit, not as an afterthought.

Type that’s comfortable to read

Body text big enough to read without zooming, line lengths that don’t stretch across the whole screen, enough space between lines. And the site should still work if someone makes the text bigger in their phone settings. A restaurant menu or a clinic’s list of services that breaks when the text is enlarged is losing exactly the people who most need to read it.

Everything works with a keyboard

Some people never use a mouse or a touchscreen. They move through a page with the Tab key or with other assistive devices. Every menu, button, form and pop-up should work that way, and you should always be able to see where you are on the page. Try it yourself: open your website, put the mouse aside and press Tab. If you get lost, so do they.

Screen readers can make sense of it

People who are blind or have low vision often use a screen reader. For it to work, the page needs real structure: proper headings, buttons that are actually buttons, links that say where they go (“See our prices” rather than “Click here”), and images with short text descriptions, called alt text. This is the same structure that helps search engines, as you’ll see in a moment.

Captions and transcripts

If you use video, add captions. They help people who are deaf or hard of hearing, and also the many people who watch with the sound off. A short transcript for a podcast or an interview does the same for audio, and gives search engines text they can read.

Dark mode, done properly

Many people set their phone to dark mode to reduce glare, save battery or simply because it’s easier on their eyes at night. A site that respects that setting feels considerate. Doing it well means more than inverting colours: contrast still has to hold, and logos and photos still have to look right.

Respecting motion sensitivity

Big parallax effects and things flying in from every side can cause discomfort or even nausea for some people. Phones and computers have a “reduce motion” setting, and a well-built site listens to it, toning down animations for those who asked. Movement should support the content, never get in the way of it.

Forms that don’t fight you

Forms are where businesses earn their money: bookings, enquiries, checkouts, sign-ups. Every field should have a visible label (not just grey placeholder text that disappears when you start typing). Errors should explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in words, not only in red. Don’t ask for more than you need. A gym membership form or a property enquiry that’s easy to complete is simply a form that converts better.

Why it’s good business, not just good manners

It helps every customer. Clear contrast, readable text and simple forms make a site easier for people in a hurry, people on small screens and people using a second language. Accessibility improvements are usability improvements.

It helps search engines and AI assistants read you. Search engines and AI tools like ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google’s AI Overviews read your website a bit like a screen reader does: through its structure and text. Clear headings, descriptive links, alt text on images and transcripts on videos give them more to understand and quote. I wrote more about this in how to get found when people ask AI instead of Google.

It reflects on your brand. A hotel, a school or a clinic that’s easy to use for everyone sends a quiet message: we thought about you. A site that shuts people out sends the opposite one, and most of them won’t tell you. They just leave, which is one of the signs I listed in 7 signs your website is costing you clients.

It’s cheaper to build in than to bolt on. Getting the structure, colours and forms right from the first design costs very little extra. Fixing them on a finished site means redoing work you’ve already paid for.

A note on rules: in many countries accessibility is also a legal expectation for some kinds of organisations, and the details vary by country and sector. I’m a designer, not a lawyer, so if that applies to you, check with someone qualified. But even where nobody requires it, it’s worth doing for the reasons above.

“Design for the person having the hardest time, and you end up with something easier for everyone.”

A checklist to bring to your designer

You don’t need to be technical to ask these. A good designer or studio should be happy to answer them clearly:

  • Do you check colour contrast against WCAG as you design?
  • Does the site still work if I make the text bigger on my phone?
  • Can someone use the whole site with only a keyboard, and can they always see where they are?
  • Are you using proper headings, buttons and link text, so screen readers can follow the page?
  • Who writes the alt text for images, and will I be able to add it myself when I upload new ones?
  • Will videos have captions? Can I add them to future videos easily?
  • Will the site support dark mode, and how will you keep contrast right in both?
  • Does the site respect the “reduce motion” setting?
  • Do all form fields have visible labels and clear error messages?
  • How will you test it: with real keyboards, screen readers and phones, not only automated tools?

If the answer to most of these is a confident yes with an explanation, you’re in good hands. If the answer is “we can add that later”, ask how, and what it will cost.

How we approach it

Every site we build by hand at True Love starts from real structure, readable type and colours we check as we go. To me, accessibility is part of building a site properly, not an afterthought. If you’re planning a new website or an app, it’s something we’ll talk about from the first conversation.

Want a site that works for everyone?

Tell us about your project in our three-minute brief and get an estimate straight away. Or, if you’d like an honest look at your current site first, get in touch.

Written by Javi Beat, founder of True Love Creative, a creative studio in Dubai making websites, brands and apps since 2015.

title: How to Write a Website Brief That Gets You an Accurate Quote
subtitle: What to prepare before you contact a designer, the mistakes that cost you time, and a shortcut that takes three minutes.
excerpt: Most quotes go wrong before any design starts. Here is what to prepare before you brief a designer or studio, the mistakes I see most often, and how our brief form asks the right questions for you.
seoTitle: How to Write a Website Brief — True Love Creative
seoDescription: What to prepare before briefing a web designer: goals, audience, examples, content, must-have features and budget. Plus the mistakes that slow projects down.
html:
Most of the quotes that go wrong go wrong before anyone opens a design file. A client writes “we need a new website, how much?”, the studio guesses, and two people walk away with completely different pictures in their heads. One imagined five pages and a contact form. The other imagined an online shop with bookings, three languages and a members area. Neither was lying. Nobody wrote anything down.

I’ve read a lot of briefs since 2015, from one-line WhatsApp messages to forty-page PDFs. The best ones are rarely the longest. They’re the ones that answer a handful of questions honestly. Here’s what those questions are, what to prepare before you contact any designer or studio, and the mistakes I see most often.

Why the brief matters more than you think

A brief does two jobs. It lets the studio give you a quote that reflects the real work, and it gives the designer something to design towards. Without it, a quote is a guess with a number on it, and the design becomes a series of “not quite” rounds that cost both sides time and patience.

A good brief doesn’t need jargon. You don’t have to know what a CMS is or how hosting works. You just need to explain your business, your customers and what success looks like. The technical translation is our job.

What to prepare before you contact anyone

1. The goal, in one sentence

Not “a modern website”. What should the website do? Get more table bookings for a restaurant. Bring in enquiries for a property agency. Sell skincare online. Make a clinic look as trustworthy online as it is in person. Help a startup look credible in front of investors.

If you have more than one goal, put them in order. “More bookings first, then show the new menu” leads to a very different homepage than the other way round.

2. Who it’s for

Describe your ideal customer as if you were telling a friend. “Busy parents in Dubai looking for after-school activities.” “Facility managers at mid-sized companies.” “Tourists deciding where to have dinner tonight, on their phone, in the street.” The more specific you are, the better the design decisions get: tone, layout, what goes first, what can wait.

3. Examples you like, and why

This is the most useful thing you can send, and the most often half-done. Two or three links to websites you like are great. But the reason matters more than the link. “I like this hotel site because the photos are huge and it feels calm” tells me something. “I like this one” tells me almost nothing, because I might love it for completely different reasons.

Examples you dislike help just as much. “Nothing that looks like a bank” rules out a whole direction in one sentence.

4. What content you already have

Do you have a logo? Brand colours? Professional photos? Written text for each page? A domain name? Be honest here, because content is where projects quietly stall. A gym with great photos and finished copy is a very different project from a gym with a logo and a plan to “write something soon”. If you need help with copy or photography, say so up front so it’s part of the plan and the quote, not a surprise in the middle.

5. The must-haves, separated from the nice-to-haves

Make two short lists. Must-haves are the things without which the site fails: online payments for a shop, a booking calendar for a salon, property listings you can update yourself, Arabic and English for a school. Nice-to-haves are the things you’d like if the budget allows: a blog, a newsletter, a live chat.

This split is gold for a studio. It lets us show you what the core project looks like and what each extra adds, instead of one big number you can’t pull apart.

One must-have that rarely makes the list but should: a site that everyone can use, whatever their eyesight or device. I explain why in accessible design is good business.

6. An honest budget

I understand why people keep their budget secret. It feels like showing your cards. But a website can be a focused one-page site or a full platform, and both are “a website”. If you tell me roughly what you planned to spend, I can tell you honestly what that buys, what I’d prioritise and where I’d hold back. If it isn’t enough for what you want, I’d rather say it on day one than after three meetings.

A range is fine. “Somewhere between X and Y” is enough to start a real conversation.

7. Timing, and why

Is there a real deadline, like a launch, an opening day or an event? Or is it “as soon as possible” because you’re tired of the old site? Both are fine, but they’re not the same. A fixed date shapes the plan. At True Love, timing depends on the design and the scope, so we agree it together after the first conversation rather than promising a number of weeks before we know the project.

The mistakes I see most often

  • Describing the solution instead of the problem. “We need a chatbot” is a solution. “People keep asking the same five questions on WhatsApp” is the problem, and there might be a simpler answer.
  • Leaving out the awkward history. If a previous agency let you down, tell me what happened. It helps me avoid repeating it.
  • Asking for “something like Apple”. Fine as a feeling. But Apple’s site works for Apple’s products and audience. Tell me what you admire about it, and I’ll work out what applies to a dental clinic.
  • Forgetting who updates the site. If you want to change prices, menus or listings yourself every week, that changes how the site is built. Mention it.
  • Hiding the budget and then rejecting every proposal on price. Everyone loses a week.
  • Sending it to ten studios at once with no detail. You’ll get ten quotes for ten different projects and no way to compare them.

A brief you can copy

If you prefer to write your own, this structure covers almost everything:

  1. What the business does, in two sentences.
  2. The main goal of the website (and the second one, if there is one).
  3. Who the ideal customer is.
  4. Two or three sites you like, and what you like about each. One you don’t, and why.
  5. The content you have and the content you need help with.
  6. Must-have features. Nice-to-have features.
  7. Rough budget range.
  8. Any real deadline.
  9. Anything else: past experiences, competitors, worries.
“A clear brief doesn’t limit the designer. It gives them something worth aiming at.”

Or let the form ask you the questions

Because most people don’t enjoy writing briefs, we built one that does the asking. Our project brief walks you through it in about three minutes. You pick what you’re building (a website, an app or both), the type of site and the features you need, plus extras like a logo if you want them. Then it asks what the project should achieve, who it’s for, the style you’re after with room for reference websites, what content you already have, how soon you need it, and anything else worth knowing.

As you choose, it shows a live estimate in dirhams, euros, pounds or dollars. It’s approximate by design: it gives you a realistic starting point, and we adjust it to your real needs after our first conversation. If you’ve already got an idea of your budget, the last step is a good place to mention it.

Whether you use the form or write your own, the point is the same: the clearer you are at the start, the more accurate the quote and the better the result. If you’re still choosing who to work with, I wrote about that in what to look for when hiring a web designer, and about pricing in how much a website costs in Dubai.

Ready to start?

Take three minutes and fill in the project brief. You’ll see an estimate straight away, and I’ll come back to you with honest next steps. Prefer to talk first? Get in touch.

Written by Javi Beat, founder of True Love Creative, a creative studio in Dubai making websites, brands and apps since 2015.

title: Will AI Replace Graphic Designers? An Honest Answer
subtitle: The tools got very good, so here’s what they still can’t do and why it matters for your business.
excerpt: I use AI in my studio every day, so this isn’t a defensive rant but an honest look at what AI changed in graphic design, what it can’t do, and why a conversation before you spend is the cheapest insurance.
html:
Short answer: no. Longer answer: it has already replaced part of the job, and pretending otherwise is how designers become irrelevant. I run a creative studio, I use AI tools every day, and this question comes up in almost every first conversation with a client now. Here is the answer I give them, without panic and without hype.

What AI has genuinely taken over

Let’s be honest about the score. By late 2026, AI is good at a whole layer of graphic design work, and pretending it isn’t helps nobody:

  • Production work. Resizing one design into forty formats, removing backgrounds, upscaling photos, matching colours across product shots. This used to be billable hours. Now it’s minutes.
  • First drafts. Moodboards, rough concepts, “show me ten directions for this poster.” The blank page is gone, and honestly, good riddance.
  • Competent but generic output. A decent social post, a passable flyer, a fine banner for a weekend sale. If “fine” is all you need, AI gives you fine for almost nothing.

I say this without bitterness, because I use all of it. The technical floor of the profession rose and the boring parts got automated. That part of the job isn’t coming back.

What it hasn’t touched

Here is what people miss: execution was never the expensive part of design. Judgement was. And judgement is exactly what a generator doesn’t have.

A real project doesn’t start with “make me something beautiful.” It starts with a business problem. A restaurant that looks cheaper than it is. A dental clinic whose leaflets get thrown away unread. A real estate agency whose brochures look identical to those of the three agencies on the same street. A gym that wants to attract professionals but still looks like a teenager’s first poster. The work is figuring out why. That means asking questions, hearing what the client doesn’t say, knowing their market, and having the spine to tell them their favourite idea is the wrong one.

“AI answers the question you typed. A designer questions the question.”

Type “elegant logo for a luxury spa” into a generator and you get an elegant logo for a luxury spa. The same one everyone else typing that sentence gets. What you don’t get is anyone asking whether “luxury” is even the right position for your spa, in your neighbourhood, at your prices, against your competitors. That conversation is the actual product. The pixels are the receipt.

The new problem: everything looks the same

There is also a newer reason professionals matter more now, not less. When every café, coach, clinic and online shop pulls from the same tools, trained on the same images, sameness becomes the default look of small business. You can see it in shop windows, in social feeds, on delivery apps. I wrote about the same effect on websites in Web Design in the Age of AI, and it hits graphic design just as hard.

Standing out used to cost extra. Now blending in is free, and standing out is the whole game. A big part of my job today is making sure a client doesn’t look like the output of a prompt. Customers notice, even if they can’t name what they’re noticing.

Talk to a designer before you spend anything

This is the part I wish more business owners knew, because it would save them real money. The most expensive design mistakes I’m asked to fix aren’t ugly logos or bad flyers. They’re decisions made before any design existed:

  • Printing thousands of menus from a generated design, then discovering the Arabic text is broken, or simply isn’t Arabic.
  • Building a whole identity on an AI logo, then finding out it’s hard to protect and a competitor has something nearly identical.
  • Spending months on beautiful social templates that bring in nobody, because the problem was the message, not the visuals.

A short conversation before any of that would have cost a fraction of the cleanup. Diagnosis before treatment is cheaper in every profession, and design is no exception. A serious studio will also tell you honestly when AI tools are enough for your case. Sometimes they are. You lose nothing by asking; you can lose a lot by guessing.

So what should you actually do?

If you run a business and you’re working out where AI fits, here is my honest playbook:

  • Use AI freely for disposable things. Internal presentations, quick mockups, a one-off story for a flash sale, testing an idea before committing to it. No shame in it. I do it too.
  • Bring in a professional for anything permanent or public. Your logo and brand identity, packaging, signage, your website. Anything printed in quantity or seen by every customer.
  • Ask before big spends. Before the print run, before the rebrand, before the ad campaign. One conversation, then decide.

The designers who do well in this era aren’t the ones refusing the tools. They’re the ones using AI for the repetitive parts and keeping the thinking human. You get the speed and the judgement, and that combination is better than either alone. It’s what you should be shopping for.

How to tell real design help from prompt-running

Whoever you hire, a few questions separate design thinking from someone who is just typing prompts on your behalf:

  • Do they ask about your customers before showing you anything? A hotel, a school and an accountancy firm need very different things from the same flyer. If nobody asks who it’s for, nobody is thinking about it.
  • Can they explain their choices? Why this typeface, this colour, this layout. “It looks nice” isn’t a reason.
  • Do you get files you can actually use? Print-ready, editable, in every format your printer, sign maker and web developer will ask for. I go into this in The Real Cost of an AI-Generated Logo.

If you want to see how I handle this in practice, here is how I approach graphic design, and the work it has led to.

Not sure if your project needs a professional?

Tell me what you’re working on. If AI tools are enough for your case, I’ll tell you so. Start a brief for an honest answer and an estimate, or just send me a message.

Written by Javi Beat, founder of True Love Creative, a creative studio in Dubai making websites, brands and apps since 2015.
seoTitle: Will AI Replace Graphic Designers? — True Love Creative
seoDescription: An honest look from a Dubai design studio at what AI now does well in graphic design, what it still cannot do, and when your business needs a professional.

title: The Real Cost of an AI-Generated Logo
subtitle: It takes thirty seconds and costs nothing, and sometimes that’s exactly what it’s worth.
excerpt: AI logo generators are everywhere and sometimes they’re fine, but there are costs the demo never shows: legal, practical and strategic. Read this before a generated logo goes on anything hard to change.
html:
Picture a food business that launched a year ago with a logo from an AI generator: thirty seconds, zero dirhams, looked great. Now it is signing its first retail deal, the distributor asks for brand files, and everything falls apart at once. It is a very common way for this story to go. This article is what I would tell that owner, written down so you can read it before that moment instead of after.

Let me be clear up front: this is not “never use AI logos.” There are cases where they’re the right call, and I’ll tell you which. But the generators advertise the thirty seconds and the zero dirhams. Nobody advertises the rest of the bill.

Cost 1: you may not fully own it

This one surprises people. In many countries, copyright protects work made by humans, and artwork generated entirely by AI sits in a grey area. Depending on the tool’s terms and where you operate, your rights over that logo may be weak or unclear. Registering it as a trademark may still be possible, but it gets harder when the mark looks like many others, which generated marks often do.

In plain terms: the logo on your signage, your packaging and your contracts might be something you can’t fully defend. For a hobby project, that hardly matters. For a business signing contracts and paying for shelf space, it’s a real risk. I’m not a lawyer and this isn’t legal advice, which is exactly the point. Before a logo goes on anything official, someone should have thought about this, and for a trademark you should speak to a specialist. Asking those questions early is part of what you pay a professional for.

Cost 2: you’re not the only one who got it

Generators draw on similar training data and respond to similar prompts. Type “minimal geometric fox logo tech startup” and you’re drawing from the same well as everyone else who typed nearly the same words. It is entirely possible for two businesses in the same city to end up with near-identical generated marks without either copying the other. The machine gave the same answer to the same question, because that’s what it’s built to do.

“A logo’s entire job is to be unmistakably yours. A generator’s entire mechanism is producing the most probable answer.”

Those two things pull in opposite directions, and no amount of clever prompting fully fixes it. The tools have improved a lot, and the images look more polished than ever. Polished is not the same as distinctive.

Cost 3: the files don’t survive real life

A logo isn’t one image. It’s a system of files that has to work everywhere: embroidered on a uniform, printed one centimetre wide on a business card, cut in vinyl for a shopfront, shown in white on a dark background, squeezed into an app icon or a favicon (the little icon in a browser tab), printed in one colour by a cheap printer in Deira. That needs clean vector files (artwork that scales to any size without going blurry), colour variants, spacing rules and simplified versions for small sizes.

Many generators hand you a single image file. Some give you a messy automatic trace. That is the moment the food business above hits the wall: the distributor asks for print-ready files and there aren’t any. The “free” logo now needed a professional rebuild, at rebuild prices, on a deadline. That’s the most expensive way to buy design: twice, and in a hurry.

The same thing happens to a clinic ordering signage for a second branch, a hotel briefing a uniform supplier, or an online shop that suddenly needs packaging. The moment the logo has to leave the screen, the gaps show.

Cost 4: nobody asked the strategy question

The deepest cost is the one you can’t see. A generator will happily give you a beautiful logo for the wrong brand. It doesn’t know your competitors all use the same blue. It doesn’t know your customers in Dubai read your name in two alphabets. It doesn’t know you plan to grow from coffee into catering next year, and that the cute coffee-cup icon will box you in. It doesn’t know a consultancy needs to look trustworthy before it looks trendy, or that a school’s crest has to speak to parents and children alike.

It executes; it doesn’t ask. As I argued in Will AI Replace Graphic Designers?, the asking is the real job. The artwork is what comes out of it.

When an AI logo is honestly fine

Credit where it’s due. I’d genuinely recommend a generated logo in these cases:

  • Testing an idea. Checking whether a side project has legs before it deserves real investment.
  • Internal or short-lived things. A padel team, an office party, a one-off event. Enjoy the free logo.
  • Placeholders before launch, as long as you know it’s a placeholder and plan to replace it before print runs, signage and trademarks come into the picture.

The trap isn’t using an AI logo. The trap is an AI logo quietly becoming permanent because it was already there.

The cheapest insurance: ask before you commit

Here is my standing advice. Before you put any logo, generated or not, on something expensive or hard to change, show it to a professional and ask three questions:

  1. Can I protect this?
  2. Will it work in every format I need, from a shop sign to a phone screen?
  3. Does it say what my business needs it to say?

That conversation is short. The problems it prevents can drag on for a long time.

If the answer is “you need the real thing”, meaning a proper identity built for your market, with files that work everywhere and a mark you can defend, that’s what brand identity work is. You can see it in projects like Jessica Morari, a coaching and wellness brand that now has one consistent look across print, social media and the web, or Julio Cuba, where the identity and the website were designed together. Not decoration, but a system built to carry a business for years.

And if your logo is solid but your website isn’t pulling its weight, start with these seven checks.

Already have a logo and not sure it will hold up?

Send it over. I’ll tell you straight what works, what doesn’t, and whether you actually need to change anything. Send me your logo, or if you already know you need a new identity, start a brief and get an estimate.

Written by Javi Beat, founder of True Love Creative, a creative studio in Dubai making websites, brands and apps since 2015.
seoTitle: The Real Cost of an AI-Generated Logo — True Love Creative
seoDescription: AI logos are fast and free, but ownership, file quality and strategy can cost you later. When a generated logo is fine and when your business needs more.

title: 7 Signs Your Website Is Costing You Clients
subtitle: Your site might be quietly turning people away, so here’s how to know and what to do about it.
excerpt: Most owners rarely look at their own website, yet every potential client checks it before they call. Seven honest checks to run on your site today, and what to do with the results.
html:
Here’s an uncomfortable fact about your website: you almost never look at it, and everyone deciding whether to hire you looks at it first. Before they call, before they message, before they walk in, they check. If something feels off, they don’t email you about it. They quietly choose someone else, and you never find out why.

After more than ten years of building and rebuilding websites, I can usually tell within a minute whether a site is helping a business or hurting it. These are the seven checks I run. Do them on your own site today, honestly, and you’ll know where you stand.

1. It’s slow on a phone

Open your site on your phone, on mobile data, not your office wifi. Count. If you’re still looking at a blank screen or a spinner after three seconds, many of your visitors have already gone. People have very little patience for slow pages, and speed is the first impression before any design is even visible. The usual culprits: huge uncompressed photos, heavy themes, and a pile of plugins (add-ons) nobody remembers installing.

2. It falls apart on a small screen

Most of your visitors are probably on a phone. For restaurants, salons, gyms and clinics, it’s nearly all of them. Tiny text you have to zoom into, buttons too small to tap, forms that fight you: each one is a person who gave up. “It technically works on mobile” isn’t the bar. The bar is: can someone standing in the street, holding a coffee, find your prices and contact you in under a minute, with one hand?

Small text and weak contrast don’t only annoy people; they shut some of them out completely. I explain why that matters for your revenue in Accessible Design Is Good Business.

3. Something on it is out of date

Last year’s menu. A “news” section whose latest post is from two years ago. Opening hours that don’t match your door. Prices from before your last increase. A team page with people who left. A property listing that sold months ago. It feels minor, but visitors read it as one loud message: nobody’s home. And if the website is abandoned, they wonder what else is. An outdated site can be worse than no site, because it advertises neglect.

4. A stranger can’t tell what you do in five seconds

Open your homepage and pretend you know nothing about your business. In five seconds, can you answer: what does this company do, for whom, and what should I do next? If the answer is buried under a vague slogan and a stock photo of a handshake, you’re losing the people who were ready to buy. A physiotherapy clinic should say it’s a physiotherapy clinic, where it is and how to book. Clarity beats cleverness every time.

5. It looks like a template, because it is one

This is the 2026 version of an old problem. It has never been easier to get a website: AI builders produce one in minutes. So the internet is now full of sites with the same layouts, the same gradients, the same three boxes of features under the same headline. Visitors have developed an instinct for it. When your site looks interchangeable, your business looks interchangeable, and interchangeable businesses end up competing on price alone. I wrote more about that trap in Web Design in the Age of AI.

6. Contacting you takes effort

Count the taps between landing on your site and actually reaching you. If your phone number isn’t tappable, if the contact form has nine fields, if WhatsApp, where so many of your customers already are, is nowhere to be found, you’re making interested people work to give you money. Some will. Most won’t.

The same goes for a hotel without a clear booking button, a consultant without a simple way to request a call, or an online shop that hides delivery costs until the last step. Every extra step loses people.

7. You don’t show up when people ask AI

Not long ago this was new. Now it’s normal. Many people ask ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude or Google’s AI Overviews (the summary at the top of search results) for recommendations instead of scrolling through links: “best paediatric dentist in Dubai Marina”, “who can build a website for my restaurant”. These tools can only recommend what they can read and understand. If your site is mostly images, with little real text, no clear structure and nothing that explains what you do and where, you’re easy to leave out of those answers.

Try it: ask an AI assistant about your type of business in your city. If you’re not mentioned, future clients are being sent somewhere else. I explain what to fix in How to Get Found When People Ask AI Instead of Google.

Scored yourself? Here’s what it means

Zero or one sign: your site is doing its job. Keep it updated and move on.

Two or three: you probably don’t need a rebuild. You need targeted fixes.

Four or more: your website is working against you, and every month of “we’ll deal with it later” costs you clients who never called.

One honest warning from someone in the business: the answer isn’t automatically “pay for a big redesign.” Sometimes it is. Sometimes it’s three small fixes. If you’re not sure which camp you’re in, that’s exactly the question to ask a professional before spending anything. A short conversation usually settles it, and you’ll know whether you’re looking at a small repair or a full rebuild.

If you do need the rebuild, here’s what websites actually cost in Dubai, how to choose who builds it and how to write a brief that gets you accurate quotes. You can also see what a hand-built website involves, or look at Estrela Photo, a portfolio built to load fast without giving up big, beautiful images.

Want a second pair of eyes on your site?

Send me your link and I’ll run these seven checks and tell you honestly what I find, including if you don’t need me. If you already know it’s time for a new site, start a brief and you’ll get an estimate.

Written by Javi Beat, founder of True Love Creative, a creative studio in Dubai making websites, brands and apps since 2015.

title: Web Design in the Age of AI: Why Handmade Still Wins
subtitle: Anyone can generate a website now, and that’s exactly the problem.
excerpt: AI builders produce a website in minutes, and they all look alike. Here’s how that changed what businesses should pay for, and why a site made by hand is worth more now, not less.
html:
Let me get something out of the way: I use AI every day. It helps me write code, test ideas and catch mistakes faster. Anyone in this industry who says they don’t is either not being straight with you or falling behind. So this isn’t one of those “AI is ruining everything” articles.

But something has happened to the web over the last couple of years, and if you’re about to invest in a website for your business, you should understand it.

Everything started to look the same

Today anyone can type a sentence into an AI website builder and have a working site in a few minutes. A huge number of people have done exactly that. What the demo videos don’t mention is that those sites look like each other. Same layouts, same gradients, same rounded cards, same big headline with the same three feature boxes underneath. The tools learned from the same patterns, so they repeat the same patterns.

People have a name for this now: AI slop. Your customers may not use the term, but they feel it. They land on a page and something whispers “template”. And a template says: this business is interchangeable with every other one. That’s a problem whether you run a dental clinic, a boutique hotel, a law firm or an online shop.

What that did to the market

Here’s the paradox. When everyone can generate a website, a generated website stops being worth much. Simply having a site no longer says anything about you, the same way having an email address stopped impressing anyone a long time ago.

What became scarce is distinctiveness. A site that could only belong to you. A site where the typography, the pace, the images and the words feel like the company behind it. That was always the point of design, but for twenty years you could get away with decent and generic. Not any more. Decent and generic is now free, instant and everywhere.

“When everyone has a website, the thing worth paying for is a website that couldn’t belong to anyone else.”

And now AI reads your site too

There’s a second shift that matters just as much. Your website isn’t only read by people any more. When someone asks ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude or Google’s AI Overviews for “a good family dentist near me” or “a property agent who handles off-plan in Dubai”, those tools read websites to build their answer.

A generated site with vague copy and a stock photo of a smiling team gives them almost nothing to work with. A site written by someone who understands your business, with clear pages for what you offer, who it’s for and where you are, gives them something to quote. Handmade, here, doesn’t mean decorative. It means considered: the structure and the words are decided by someone who knows what your customers ask. More on that in How to Get Found When People Ask AI Instead of Google.

What AI is genuinely good at

Credit where it’s due. In my studio, AI has changed how I work:

  • Speed. Repetitive technical work goes much faster than it used to. That saving goes into the parts of the project that need a person.
  • Exploration. I can try several directions in the time it used to take to build one. Bad ideas die sooner, and the good one gets more attention.
  • Quality checks. Testing, accessibility checks (making sure everyone can use the site, including people with poor eyesight or who use screen readers), speed audits. The boring, important work gets done more thoroughly.

Notice what isn’t on that list: taste. Deciding what a brand should feel like. Knowing when a page needs less, not more. Sitting with a client, whether that’s a wellness coach, a photographer, a restaurant owner or a startup founder, and understanding what makes them different before a single pixel exists. AI carries out instructions. It doesn’t care. Caring is the job.

How to tell the difference when you’re buying

If you’re hiring someone to build your site, the question is no longer “can they build a website?” Everyone can. The questions that matter now:

  • Does their portfolio look like one template in different colours? If every project has the same layout, you’re looking at a template operation. Human or AI, it doesn’t matter.
  • Do they ask about your business before talking about pages? Design decisions should come from who you are and who your customers are, not from whatever the tool suggests first.
  • Can they explain why, not just what? Anyone can show you a nice page. Ask why the text is that size, why the page opens that way, why the button says what it says. If there’s no answer, there was no thinking.
  • Is it built for you, or assembled for you? A site built by hand, without templates or page builders, can be shaped exactly around your content. One assembled from ready-made blocks has to squeeze your business into someone else’s shape.

I wrote a longer guide: what to look for when hiring a web designer in Dubai. All of it applies twice over now. And whoever you hire, a clear brief saves both sides a lot of guesswork, so here’s how to write one.

Where I’ve landed

I’ve been designing websites for more than ten years, and I’ve never been more sure about the value of doing it by hand. Not by hand as in refusing the tools. By hand as in every decision passes through a person who knows your name, has heard your story, and would be embarrassed if the result looked like everyone else’s.

That’s how every website we make is built: no templates, no page builders, and no timeline pulled out of a hat. How long it takes depends on the design and the scope, and we agree it together after the first conversation.

AI made average free. It made remarkable more valuable than it has ever been. That isn’t a threat to good design. It’s the best argument for it.

Want a website that couldn’t belong to anyone else?

Tell me about your project and I’ll tell you honestly what it needs, and what it doesn’t. Start a brief and you’ll see an estimate as you go.

Written by Javi Beat, founder of True Love Creative, a creative studio in Dubai making websites, brands and apps since 2015.

title: How to Get Found When People Ask AI Instead of Google
subtitle: Your next client might never see a results page, so here is how to stay visible when an AI does the recommending.
excerpt: More people now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI Overviews for recommendations. If AI can’t read your website, you don’t exist in that conversation. Here’s what any business can do about it.
html:
Ask a few people how they found the last restaurant they booked, the last clinic they visited or the last accountant they hired. A few years ago the answer was always “I googled it.” Now you hear “I asked ChatGPT” just as often. Or Perplexity, or Claude, or the assistant built into their phone.

Even the people who still google don’t see what they used to. Google’s AI Overviews answer the question at the top of the page, before a single website link. Plenty of searches now end without anyone clicking anything. The industry calls it zero-click search. I call it the biggest change to being found online since Google itself.

By late 2026 this isn’t a trend to watch. It’s simply how a large part of your future clients look for things. So the question for any business owner is practical: when someone asks an AI about what you do, does your name come up?

What actually changed

The old game was simple. Rank on page one, get the click, make your case on your own website. The new game has an extra player in the middle. An AI reads a lot of websites, forms an answer and recommends. Your future client may hear about you, or not, from a machine that read your website on their behalf.

That has a hard consequence: if AI can’t read your site, you don’t exist in that conversation. Many sites, especially the ones thrown together with page builders, are genuinely hard for these systems to understand. Text locked inside images. No clear structure. Vague copy that never says plainly what the business does, where it works or roughly what it costs.

Think of a dental clinic in Jumeirah whose homepage says “Your smile, our passion” and nothing else above the fold. A person might scroll and work it out. An assistant asked “good family dentist near Jumeirah that’s open on Saturdays” has nothing to quote.

The good news

What surprised me when I started working on this for clients is how little of it is new. Almost everything that works is honest, old-fashioned clarity. AI assistants recommend businesses they can understand and check. So the checklist looks like this.

1. Say what you do in plain words

“Family-run Italian restaurant in Dubai Marina, open since 2018, with a terrace and a set lunch on weekdays” beats “a culinary journey like no other” every time. An AI can quote the first sentence. It can do nothing with the second. The same goes for a gym, a law firm, a property agent or a software startup.

2. Answer real questions on your site

When someone asks an assistant “how much does a website cost in Dubai?” or “does this hotel allow pets?”, it looks for pages that answer exactly that. Publish your prices or price ranges, your process, your opening hours, your FAQ. That’s why I wrote an honest piece on what a website costs in Dubai instead of hiding behind “contact us for a quote.” Businesses that hide information become invisible.

3. Add structured data

Structured data is a machine-readable label inside your site: your name, address, services, opening hours, prices and reviews, written in a format search engines and assistants trust. Your visitors never see it. For machines, it’s often the clearest thing on the page.

4. Keep pages fast, clean and readable

AI crawlers give up on slow, bloated pages even faster than people do. A site that is built properly, with real headings, real text and clean code, is readable by everything. That’s the whole point of building it by hand rather than stacking plugins.

5. Make it accessible

The things that help a screen reader help an AI too: proper headings, descriptive links, text alternatives for images. I wrote more about this in why accessible design is good business. It’s the rare piece of work that pays off twice.

6. Be mentioned elsewhere

Assistants cross-check. Reviews on Google, listings in the directories that matter for your industry, press, partners and clients linking to you. If the only place you exist is your own website, you’re a rumour, not a fact.

“AI search rewards the businesses with nothing to hide and quietly ignores the ones hiding behind buzzwords.”

What I do on every site I build

Every website that leaves the studio ships with the basics done properly: structured data that describes the business, semantic markup, a sitemap, fast load times, and copy written to answer the questions clients actually ask. Some of it, like an llms.txt file (a plain summary written specifically for AI crawlers), barely existed a few years ago. This site has one.

None of this is magic, and be wary of anyone selling it as magic. There is no secret trick that makes ChatGPT recommend you, and nobody can guarantee you’ll appear in a particular answer. There is only being findable, readable and worth recommending. Many businesses in Dubai still haven’t covered the basics. That’s the opportunity.

A quick self-check

Try this today. It takes ten minutes.

  1. Ask two or three AI assistants a question your ideal client would ask, the way they’d ask it. “Best physiotherapy clinic in Al Barsha for sports injuries.” “Who designs restaurant menus in Dubai?”
  2. See who gets named. If it isn’t you, open the sites that were named and compare them with yours.
  3. Read your own homepage as if you were a stranger. Can you tell, in one sentence, what you do, where and for whom?
  4. Check whether your prices, hours and contact details are written as text, not hidden in a PDF or an image.

If that last check made you wince, my list of signs your website is costing you clients is a good next read.

The part nobody wants to hear

Visibility gets you into the conversation. It doesn’t win it. When an assistant gives someone three options and they open yours, you have a few seconds of human attention. Then it’s back to the oldest question there is: does this site make me trust these people?

That’s design, and it’s the part no machine does for you. Getting found is the new front door. People still buy from people.

Is your website invisible to AI?

Tell me about your business and your site in a short brief. I’ll take an honest look and tell you where you stand, with no jargon and no scare tactics. If you’d rather just talk, get in touch.

Written by Javi Beat, founder of True Love Creative, a creative studio in Dubai making websites, brands and apps since 2015.

title: What to Look for When Hiring a Web Designer in Dubai
subtitle: Red flags, smart questions and how to tell good from great before you sign anything.
excerpt: You searched “web designer Dubai” and now you’re drowning in options. Here’s how to tell who actually delivers, from someone who has been designing and building websites in Dubai since 2015.
html:
You’ve decided you need a website. You’ve searched “web designer Dubai”, or asked an AI assistant, and now you’re drowning in options. Agencies, freelancers, “full-service digital solutions”. Beautiful portfolios, big claims, five-star reviews that all sound strangely alike. And you’re thinking: how do I actually tell who’s good?

I’ve been designing and building websites in Dubai since 2015, and I’ve been on both sides of the table: hiring creatives and being hired as one. This is the guide I wish someone had handed me the first time I hired a designer. It works whether you run a restaurant, a clinic, a property agency, an online shop or a startup that hasn’t launched yet.

The Dubai problem

Dubai has too much of everything. You’ll find agencies with glass offices and large teams quoting AED 50,000 or more. You’ll find marketplace freelancers charging AED 500 for a template with your logo dropped in. And in late 2026 you’ll also find people selling sites generated by AI builders in an afternoon, which look exactly like everybody else’s.

Everyone says “award-winning” and “results-driven”. Every portfolio looks great, because portfolios are curated. The real question isn’t who looks good on paper. It’s who actually delivers. Here’s how to find out.

Look at live sites, not mockups

If a designer only shows you Figma screens, Behance shots or PDFs, be careful. A mockup is a promise. A live website is proof.

Ask for links. Open them on your phone. Check how fast they load. Find the contact page. Fill in a form. If a designer can’t point you to real, working websites, that tells you a lot.

When someone asks me for examples, I send them to live projects like Jessica Morari, a coaching and wellness brand, or Estrela Photo, a photography portfolio. Real sites, live right now. Click through, resize the window, test the speed. That’s the standard I hold myself to, and it’s the one you should hold any designer to. You can see the rest in the work section.

Ask who actually does the work

This catches people off guard. You meet an agency. The person across the table is polished and says all the right things. You sign. Then you never hear from that person again, and your project is handed to a team you’ve never met.

Remote teams aren’t the problem. Some of the best developers I know work from other continents. But you should know who is designing and building your site, and you should be able to talk to them. When the person selling the project and the people doing it never overlap, things get lost.

With True Love, you work with me directly. I’m the one who designs it, who builds it, and who answers your message when something needs fixing before launch.

Ask how they use AI

This is the new question, and a fair one. Almost every studio uses AI tools now, me included. That’s fine. What matters is whether AI is helping skilled people work better, or replacing the thinking you’re paying for.

Ask them straight: what do you use it for, and what do you never hand over to it? A good answer is specific. A vague or defensive one is a warning. I wrote about this in more depth in web design in the age of AI.

Check the tech, not just the design

A beautiful website that takes eight seconds to load is not doing its job. Visitors leave before they read a word, and search engines notice.

Ask about speed. Ask about mobile. Ask about SEO, the real kind. Can they explain what structured data is? Do they know what a Lighthouse score measures? And now: what do they do so that AI assistants can read and recommend the site? If that last question gets a blank look, read how to get found in AI search before you sign anything.

A simple test: run one of their live sites through Google PageSpeed Insights. A low score on mobile means they aren’t paying attention to what matters. On my own sites, I treat a low score as a bug to fix, not a detail.

Read the contract before you pay

I’ve heard the horror stories from clients who came to me afterwards. A business that wanted to change hosting and found the agency “owned” the code. “Unlimited revisions” that turned out to mean three rounds, buried in the small print. A monthly maintenance fee for a site that didn’t need maintaining.

Before you sign, make sure you know:

  • How many revisions are included, and what counts as one.
  • Who owns the code, the design and the domain when it’s finished.
  • What happens after launch: is there a handover, and what support is included?
  • What the payment schedule looks like: deposit, milestones, final payment.
  • Whether there are any recurring fees you didn’t expect.

A good designer is upfront about all of this before you even ask. If they’re vague about money, they’ll be vague about everything else.

Be wary of fixed timelines before anyone understands your project

Some studios promise “your site in two weeks” before they know anything about your business. Speed isn’t bad, but a timeline given before the first real conversation is a sales line, not a plan. How long a site takes depends on the design, the scope and how ready your content is. A serious designer agrees the timing with you once they understand what you need.

The longevity test

Don’t stop at screenshots. Visit the actual sites from their portfolio, including older ones.

Are they still live? Do they still look good? Are they still fast? A designer with five great sites that are still running years later is worth more than one with fifty that are broken, offline or frozen in 2019. If most of someone’s past work has disappeared, ask why.

Price is not quality

I wrote a whole article about how much a website costs in Dubai, so I won’t repeat it here. The short version: expensive doesn’t automatically mean good, and very cheap almost always means corners were cut.

A large agency quote often pays for offices, sales teams and account managers as much as for your website. The AED 500 option usually gives you a template and hope. What you want is someone with real experience and a portfolio of live work, who isn’t carrying heavy overhead, and who is honest enough to tell you what you actually need rather than what makes the invoice bigger.

Trust your gut

If communication is poor before you’ve paid, it will be worse after. If they take five days to reply while they’re trying to win you, imagine waiting for an urgent fix on your live site.

Notice how they talk to you. Do they ask about your business, or only talk about themselves? Do they listen? Do they explain things clearly, or hide behind jargon? A website project is a working relationship. You should enjoy it.

I’ve turned down projects when the fit wasn’t right, and I’d rather a client told me honestly we weren’t a match than have us both pretend.

“A good designer doesn’t just build what you ask for. They tell you what you actually need.”

Red flags checklist

  • Only mockups, no live links
  • Won’t say who designs and builds the site
  • No mention of speed, SEO or AI visibility
  • Vague contract or surprise fees
  • A fixed timeline before they understand your project
  • Slow replies before you’ve paid
  • Portfolio sites that are offline or broken
  • Can’t explain how they use AI, or what they use to build

Frequently asked

How do I check if a web designer is good?

Ask for live links, not mockups. Open their sites on your phone. Run them through Google PageSpeed Insights. Check that older projects are still live and working. That tells you more than any pitch.

Is it better to hire an agency or a freelancer in Dubai?

Neither is automatically better. Agencies carry overhead that pushes prices up. The cheapest freelancers cut corners. Often the best option is an experienced independent studio where you deal directly with the person doing the work.

What should a web design contract include?

Revisions, ownership of code, design and domain, the payment schedule, what support you get after launch, and any recurring fees. If any of these are vague, ask before you sign.

How long does it take to build a website?

It depends on the design and the scope: a single landing page and an online shop with bookings are very different projects. A good designer agrees the timing with you after the first conversation, not before.

What should I prepare before talking to a designer?

A short description of your business, who you want to reach, a few sites you like and why, and a rough budget. My guide on how to write a website brief walks you through it.

Ready to talk about your project?

Fill in the project brief. It takes a few minutes and gives you a live estimate as you go. Or get in touch and I’ll give you an honest answer, not a sales pitch.

Written by Javi Beat, founder of True Love Creative, a creative studio in Dubai making websites, brands and apps since 2015.

title: How Much Does a Website Cost in Dubai?
subtitle: An honest look at market prices, what moves the number and where my studio sits.
excerpt: Everyone asks it, most agencies dodge it. Here’s what websites cost across the Dubai market, why the range is so wild, which hidden costs to ask about, and how to get a real number for your project.
html:
Everyone asks this, and it’s usually the first question. Before “what’s your process” or “can I see your work”, it’s straight to: how much? I understand. You’re running a business, you need to budget, and too many agencies make you fill in a form and wait days for a PDF that still doesn’t give you a number.

So here is an honest answer, from someone who has been quoting websites in Dubai since 2015. First what the market looks like, then what moves the price, then where my studio sits.

Why the range is so wild

Search “website cost Dubai” and you’ll find quotes from AED 500 to AED 500,000. That isn’t helpful on its own. The reason is simple: “website” can mean a hundred different things. A template with your logo on it is a website. So is a custom platform with user accounts, online payments and a content system your team updates every day. Same word, completely different products.

It’s a bit like asking how much a car costs. The honest answer starts with “what do you need it to do?”

What you’ll find on the market

These are rough starting points you’ll see across Dubai, from freelancers and small studios up to large agencies. They’re market context, not my prices, and every provider counts differently.

Type of projectWhat it isTypical market starting point
Template siteA ready-made theme with your logo and colours swapped inFrom around AED 500
Landing pageOne scrolling page: who you are, what you offer, how to contact youAround AED 1,500–2,000 at the budget end
Business website (5–10 pages)Services, about, work or menu, contact, set up for searchFrom around AED 3,000 at the budget end
Online shopProduct catalogue, cart, payments, stockFrom around AED 5,500 at the budget end
Mobile app (iOS / Android)A real app that goes on the App Store and Google PlayFrom around AED 15,000
Large agency projectStrategy, big teams, account managementOften AED 40,000–50,000 and well beyond

Notice the words “at the budget end”. Those figures usually mean a lighter build, a theme underneath or fewer rounds of design. A custom site designed from scratch costs more than the floor of the market, and it should.

What affects the price

Whoever you hire, a few things move the number:

  • Number of pages and sections. More pages means more design and more building. A dental clinic with five treatments needs less than a hotel with rooms, restaurants, events and offers.
  • Custom features. Bookings, online payments, member areas, property listings with filters, multi-language content. Anything beyond static pages adds work.
  • Content. Do you have your text and photos ready, or do they need to be written and shot? Copywriting and photography are usually quoted separately.
  • Brand. If you don’t have a logo and visual identity yet, that’s a separate job, and it’s worth doing first. See brand identity.
  • Languages. In Dubai, English and Arabic is common. A second language, especially one that reads right to left, is real design and development work, not just translation.
  • Animations and interactions. Subtle motion adds polish, but getting it right takes time.
  • Tight deadlines. If it has to go live for a specific date, say so early. Squeezing a project usually costs more.

The cheap option trap

You can get a website for AED 500. Someone will take a template, change the colours, add your logo and hand it over. It will look like exactly that, and it will look like hundreds of other sites. In 2026 the same is true of sites spat out by AI builders in minutes.

I regularly meet business owners who paid twice: once for the cheap version that didn’t bring in a single enquiry, and again to do it properly. That isn’t saving money. It’s spending double. If you’re not sure whether your current site is working, run through these signs your website is costing you clients.

A website isn’t really an expense. It’s often the first thing a client sees before they call you, and that first impression decides whether they call at all.

“You don’t get a second first impression.”

Hidden costs to ask about

The build price isn’t the whole picture. Before you compare quotes, ask each provider about:

  • Domain and hosting. Who pays, how much per year, and whose name are they in?
  • Monthly fees. Some providers add maintenance or “platform” fees for sites that barely need them.
  • Licences. Paid themes, plugins, fonts and stock photos can carry yearly costs.
  • Changes after launch. What does it cost to add a page or update prices six months from now?
  • Ownership. If you leave, do you take the code and content with you?

Where True Love sits

My studio sits between the template sellers and the big agencies. Not a marketplace freelancer, not a large agency charging for its office rent. You work directly with me, and every site is designed and built by hand.

Web design starts from AED 8,000. What you end up paying depends on the scope: the pages, the features, the content and the languages. Rather than guess, the quickest way to get a real number is to fill in the project brief, which shows you a live estimate as you answer. After that, I send you a clear quote so there are no surprises.

Every project includes:

  • Custom design. No templates, no themes, no page builders. Designed from scratch for your business.
  • Responsive build. It works properly on every screen, from a phone to a large monitor.
  • Search and AI visibility. Proper metadata, structured data, a sitemap and fast loading, so both search engines and AI assistants can read you. More in how to get found in AI search.
  • Performance. Clean, hand-written code. Your site will be fast.
  • Handover. You own it: domain, code and content.

Need an app rather than a website? That’s priced once it’s scoped. See app development.

Frequently asked

How long does a website take?

It depends on the design and the scope, and on how quickly the content is ready. We agree the timing together after the first conversation, once I understand what you need.

Do I pay everything upfront?

No. Payment is split into stages, starting with a deposit. The exact split is set out in your quote, and larger projects can be divided into milestones.

Can I update the site myself?

Yes. I can set up a simple way for you to edit text and images without touching code. Or, if you’d rather not deal with it, I can handle updates for you.

Do you work with clients outside Dubai?

All the time. Most of the work happens remotely, and I work with clients across the Gulf and Europe. What matters is good communication, not location.

How do I get an accurate quote?

Tell me what you need. A clear brief gets you a clear number. My guide on how to write a website brief helps, and so does knowing what to look for in a web designer.

Ready to see a real number?

Fill in the project brief and you’ll see an estimate as you go. You’ll get a real answer, with timing and price, within 24 hours. Prefer to talk first? Get in touch.

title: Why Every DJ, Musician and Performer Needs a Professional Website
subtitle: Instagram is not your website, and for anyone who gets booked as a person, that matters.
excerpt: Thousands of followers and zero control over your brand. Why DJs, musicians and every kind of performer need a site of their own, what it should include, and why AI assistants now make it matter more.
html:
This might sting a little. You have thousands of followers, your mixes get shared, you play good venues. And when someone searches your name, what comes up? An Instagram profile, maybe a SoundCloud page. That’s your whole online identity, and you don’t own any of it.

I know this because I’m a DJ myself, playing in Dubai. Over the years I’ve also built websites for musicians like Kiko Navarro, Manuel KevSax, Sergio Trumpet and Julio Cuba. I’ve seen what changes when an artist gets a proper site.

This post talks mostly about DJs and musicians, because that’s where I see it most. But it applies just as much to anyone who is booked or hired as a person: singers, dancers, magicians, hosts and MCs, photographers, speakers, coaches, make-up artists, chefs who do private events. If people book you, read on.

Instagram is rented land

Instagram, TikTok, SoundCloud: none of them are yours. The algorithm changes and your reach drops overnight. An account gets hacked or flagged and years of posts disappear. It happens, including to people with very large followings.

Your website is your land. You decide what goes on it, how it looks and what people see first. No algorithm choosing whether your work gets shown. No competing with memes for attention. Someone types your name, and they find you.

Social media is still where people discover you. Keep it. Just make sure it points somewhere you control.

The booking question

Here’s how it plays out. A hotel events manager is putting together a season of live music and needs a saxophonist. Someone recommends a name. The manager searches it.

Scenario A: they find an Instagram profile. They scroll, watch a reel, can’t find booking details. They send a DM. Maybe it’s seen, maybe not. They move on to the next name.

Scenario B: they find a site like Manuel KevSax’s. Professional photos, video, a clear list of past venues and a booking form. They fill it in in two minutes.

Which one do you think gets the call back first?

The same scene happens with a wedding planner looking for a violinist, a brand looking for a photographer like Estrela Photo, or someone choosing a wellness coach like Jessica Morari. The people who make hiring decisions want to check you quickly, in one place, and feel sure.

AI is now part of the booking

In late 2026, that events manager might not even search. They might ask ChatGPT or another assistant: “recommend a live saxophonist in Dubai for a hotel brunch.” Assistants answer by reading websites. An Instagram grid gives them very little to go on. A clear website with your name, what you do, where you perform and who you’ve played for gives them something to quote.

I explain how this works in how to get found when people ask AI instead of Google. The short version: if you only exist on social media, you’re much harder to recommend.

What I’ve seen happen

When I built Kiko Navarro’s website, the goal wasn’t just a nice page. Kiko has been producing and performing for decades, and his online presence didn’t reflect that. Now, when a promoter, a label or a journalist looks him up, they find a site that matches who he is. That changes how people approach an artist.

I’ve seen the same with other performers I’ve worked with. A proper site moves the first message from “how much for a gig?” towards “we’d love to work with you, what’s your availability?” It doesn’t replace talent or reputation. It makes them visible.

What a performer’s website actually needs

It doesn’t need to be complicated. A good site for a DJ, musician or any performer has:

  • A strong visual identity. Your brand, not a generic template. The site should feel the way your work feels. If you don’t have an identity yet, start with branding.
  • A bio and press kit. A short bio, a longer one, high-resolution photos people can download, and your key highlights. Make life easy for whoever is booking you.
  • Your work, front and centre. Embedded mixes and tracks, live clips, a photo gallery, a showreel. Let the work speak.
  • A booking form. Not a DM, not “link in bio”. A real form that asks for the date, the venue and the type of event, so you get useful enquiries.
  • Upcoming dates and past venues. If you’re playing or appearing somewhere, show it. Proof matters in this business.
  • Clear, readable text. Who you are, what you do and where you work, written in plain words, so both people and AI assistants understand you.

For artwork, covers, posters and social graphics that match the site, see graphic design. You can also look at my own DJ site to see how I do it for myself.

The investment

A professional website is an investment, and it’s worth being clear about what it costs. I wrote an honest breakdown of website prices in Dubai, and my own web design starts from AED 8,000. The best way to get a number for your project is the project brief, which gives you an estimate as you go.

Unlike a single gig, a website keeps working when you’re not. It’s there when the promoter looks you up at 2am, and when someone in another country hears your mix and wants to know more.

I’ve been on both sides of this, as a DJ who needed a site and as the person who builds them. It’s one of the few things in this career that keeps working for you long after it’s done.

“Your website is your stage when you’re not on stage.”

Written by Javi Beat, founder of True Love Creative, a creative studio in Dubai making websites, brands and apps since 2015.
